prompt: moto answers run-instances with an instance id. What is behind that id?
hint: moto runs nothing.

choices.text: A container that moto starts on your computer for each instance
choices.why: moto starts no container. The lessons that run code for real use Docker themselves, outside moto.

choices.text: A record in moto's memory
choices.why: Right. It has an id and a state, and it is forgotten when moto stops.

choices.text: A small virtual machine that moto boots with QEMU
choices.why: There is no machine behind the id at all, virtual or otherwise.

choices.text: A real instance in a sandbox account that AWS lends to moto
choices.why: Nothing in this course reaches AWS. moto answers from your own computer.

prompt: In a new terminal, aws sts get-caller-identity fails with InvalidClientTokenId. Who refused the request?
hint: Which line does a new terminal forget?

choices.text: AWS itself: without AWS_ENDPOINT_URL the request went to the real service
choices.why: Right. Nothing was created and nothing was billed, and it is why no real key goes into this command line.

choices.text: moto, because it does not accept test and test as a key pair from this terminal
choices.why: moto accepts test. It is AWS that does not know the word.

choices.text: moto, because it had been stopped
choices.why: A stopped moto gives a different error: the command line cannot connect to the endpoint at all.

choices.text: The laptop's firewall, which blocks port 4567
choices.why: A firewall would stop the connection; this answer came back from a server that read the request.

prompt: Stopping moto_server with Ctrl+C ___ it, which is why every lesson starts from nothing.
hint: What happens to what it kept in memory?

prompt: Why does prices.py name one published version of each offer instead of reading the current one?
hint: What would change between two runs a year apart?

choices.text: Because AWS deletes old versions of the price list after a year
choices.why: The opposite: AWS keeps every version it ever published, which is what makes pinning possible.

choices.text: Because the current version needs an AWS key
choices.why: No version needs a key. The price list is public, current and old alike.

choices.text: To make the EC2 download smaller
choices.why: A pinned version of the EC2 offer is the same size as any other, about 290 MB.

choices.text: So that it prints the same sheet whenever it is run
choices.why: Right. Prices move; a pinned file does not, so the numbers in the lessons stay true.

prompt: A download of the EC2 file is cut halfway through. What is left in the cache, and what happens next?
hint: Where does the download go before it is renamed?

choices.text: Half a JSON file, which the next run reads and fails on
choices.why: That is the failure the .part file exists to prevent: nothing is renamed until it is complete.

choices.text: A .part file only; the next run starts it again
choices.why: Right. The run stopped with ContentTooShortError, and no half file looks finished.

choices.text: Nothing; the next run resumes from the byte where it stopped
choices.why: The program does not resume a download. It starts the file again.

choices.text: The previous complete file, which the program keeps as a backup
choices.why: There is no previous file for a version never downloaded; each version gets its own name.

prompt: The sheet prices an EKS cluster with standard support at 0.1 USD per hour. What does one cluster cost for a month of 730 hours, in USD?
hint: Hourly price times 730.

prompt: Match each piece of the name m7gd.2xlarge to what it says.
hint: Family, generation, processor, extra, size.

pairs.right: Twice the vCPU and memory of an xlarge

prompt: Compared with c7g.xlarge, what does the n in c7gn.xlarge add?
hint: Look at the last column of the first table.

choices.text: A local NVMe disk of 237 GB
choices.why: That is the d, in c7gd.xlarge.

choices.text: A newer generation of the same hardware
choices.why: The generation is the number, 7 in all three.

choices.text: 40 gigabits of network instead of 12.5
choices.why: Right. Processor, memory and storage stay the same.

choices.text: Twice the memory per vCPU
choices.why: Memory per vCPU is set by the family letter, c, and is the same in the three.

prompt: m7i.large and m7g.large both have 2 vCPU. What differs between those two vCPU?
hint: Cores and threads per core.

choices.text: On m7i they are whole cores, and on m7g they are threads that share a core
choices.why: The reverse. Graviton has no second thread; Intel runs two per core.

choices.text: Nothing: a vCPU is one core on every type
choices.why: On Intel types a vCPU is a thread, and two of them share one core.

choices.text: m7g has half the memory to go with them
choices.why: Both have 8 GiB. The family letter m fixes the ratio for both.

choices.text: On m7i they are two threads of one core; on m7g, two whole cores
choices.why: Right. moto's table shows 1 core with 2 threads against 2 cores with 1 thread.

prompt: moto accepted run-instances for an m7g.large from an x86_64 image. What does AWS do with the same request?
hint: When does EC2 check the pair?

choices.text: Refuses it before anything starts
choices.why: Right. The image's architecture has to match the type's, and moto does not check it.

choices.text: Launches it, and the instance fails at boot, billed for the time it ran
choices.why: EC2 checks the architecture before launching, so nothing starts and nothing is billed.

choices.text: Launches it and runs the x86 code under emulation, more slowly
choices.why: EC2 does not emulate one instruction set on another.

choices.text: Launches an m7i.large instead, the nearest x86 type
choices.why: EC2 never changes the type you asked for. It launches that type or refuses.

prompt: Older generations carry no processor letter when the processor is from ___, as in m5.large.
hint: m5a.large is the AMD one.

prompt: Going by r7i.large, how much memory per vCPU does the memory-optimised family give?
hint: 16 GiB for 2 vCPU.

choices.text: 2 GiB
choices.why: That is c, compute optimised.

choices.text: 4 GiB
choices.why: That is m, general purpose.

choices.text: 8 GiB
choices.why: Right: 16 GiB over 2 vCPU.

choices.text: 16 GiB
choices.why: 16 GiB is the whole machine, for two vCPU.

prompt: Three copies of a service move from m7i.xlarge (0.3213 USD an hour) to r7i.large (0.21105). How much is saved in a month of 730 hours, in USD?
hint: The difference per hour, times 730, times three.

prompt: Which of these does describe-instance-types or describe-instance-type-offerings against moto tell you truthfully? Choose all that apply.
hint: moto carries a copy of AWS's data, and measures nothing.

choices.text: The vCPU and memory of i4i.large
choices.why: Specifications come from AWS's own data.

choices.text: The size of c7gd.xlarge's local disk
choices.why: 237 GB, from the same data.

choices.text: The hourly price of m7i.large in São Paulo
choices.why: Neither command carries a price; prices come from the public price list.

choices.text: Which zones of sa-east-1 offer i4i.large
choices.why: The offerings are AWS's too, as of that moto release.

choices.text: How busy the processor of your instance is
choices.why: moto keeps no metrics; that measurement is CloudWatch's on AWS.

prompt: Order these types from the least memory per vCPU to the most.
hint: Divide memory by vCPU; x2idn.16xlarge is 64 vCPU and 1,024 GiB.
trap: x2idn.16xlarge looks largest because of its size, and it is last for its ratio, 16 GiB per vCPU, not for its total.

prompt: A cache needs 14 GiB of memory and barely uses its processor, and the software has Arm builds. Which type on the sheet fits it at the lowest hourly price?
hint: Fit first, then the cheapest of what fits.

choices.text: r7i.large, at 0.21105
choices.why: It fits, but its Graviton twin has the same 16 GiB for 0.1704.

choices.text: c7g.large, the cheapest Graviton type at 0.1111 an hour
choices.why: It has 4 GiB. The cheapest machine that does not fit is no answer.

choices.text: r7g.large, 16 GiB for 0.1704
choices.why: Right: memory optimised for the ratio, Graviton for the price.

choices.text: m7i.xlarge, which also has 16 GiB, at 0.3213
choices.why: It pays for four vCPU the cache does not use.

prompt: m7i.2xlarge costs 0.6426 USD an hour. What does it cost for a month of 730 hours, in USD, to the cent?
hint: Hourly price times 730.

prompt: Two m7i.large or one m7i.xlarge: what does the price sheet say about the difference?
hint: 0.16065 twice, against 0.3213.

choices.text: The xlarge is cheaper per vCPU, a discount for buying bigger
choices.why: There is no such discount inside a family: the price doubles exactly with the size.

choices.text: Nothing: two larges cost exactly what one xlarge costs, hour for hour
choices.why: Right. The choice is about failure and the size of each step, not about money.

choices.text: Two larges cost more, because each instance pays a fixed fee
choices.why: EC2 on demand has no fee per instance; it is the hourly price and nothing else.

choices.text: The xlarge costs four times as much, for twice the machine
choices.why: 0.3213 is twice 0.16065, not four times.

prompt: moto's catalogue says m7i.large has "Up to 12.5 Gigabit" of network. What does that mean?
hint: Compare the baseline column with the peak column.

choices.text: 12.5 gigabits a second, sustained for as long as you need
choices.why: Only from 8xlarge does the baseline reach 12.5. Below that it is a peak.

choices.text: A guaranteed 0.781 gigabits, with bursts up to 12.5 for a while
choices.why: Right. A small size can be held back by the network before its processor is busy.

choices.text: 12.5 gigabits shared between every instance on the same host
choices.why: The figure is per instance, and the baseline is the part guaranteed to it.

choices.text: The bandwidth to EBS, not to the network
choices.why: EBS bandwidth is listed apart, though it follows the same pattern.

prompt: A t3.medium earns 24 credits an hour and holds at most 576. It runs both vCPU at 35%. Starting from a full balance, how many hours until the credits are gone?
hint: Credits spent per hour: 35% of two vCPU for sixty minutes.

prompt: moto reported CpuCredits standard for a t3.medium launched with unlimited. What does AWS do with a t3 launched with no credit specification at all?
hint: AWS's documentation, not moto's answer.

choices.text: Launches it in unlimited mode
choices.why: Right. Surplus above the baseline is billed rather than throttled.

choices.text: Launches it in standard mode, as moto reported
choices.why: moto's answer is its own. AWS's default for t3, t3a and t4g is the other mode.

choices.text: Refuses the request until a mode is chosen
choices.why: The specification is optional; leaving it out picks the default.

choices.text: Launches it in standard mode and switches to unlimited when the credits run out
choices.why: The mode does not switch on its own; it is a setting that stays until changed.

prompt: One CPU credit pays for one vCPU at 100% for one ___.
hint: It is why 20% of two vCPU earns 24 an hour.

prompt: A staging server averages 5% CPU and, a few times a day, runs a build at 100% on both vCPU for 20 minutes. It needs 4 GiB. Which is the better buy?
hint: A build costs 40 credits; the baseline earns 24 an hour.

choices.text: c7i.large, because builds need the whole processor
choices.why: It pays for the whole processor all day to use it an hour a day.

choices.text: m7g.large, since Graviton costs a fifth less than Intel
choices.why: It is cheaper than m7i, not than t3.medium, and it carries 8 GiB nobody needs.

choices.text: m7i.large, because general purpose is the safe default
choices.why: The safe default is for a service with nothing measured. This one is measured, and idle.

choices.text: t3.medium, at less than half the price of c7i.large
choices.why: Right. It sits far under its 20% baseline, and the credits it earns pay for the builds.

prompt: Put the steps of moving a service from m7i.large to m7g.large in a sensible order.
hint: What could stop the move should be found first.
items: Check that every dependency has an arm64 build
Build or choose an arm64 image
Launch an m7g.large from it and test under real load
Replace the m7i instances one by one
trap: Launching before checking the image is the step AWS's architecture check refuses, and moto lets through.

prompt: Ten instances move from c7i.large (0.13755 USD an hour) to c7g.large (0.1111). How much is saved in a month of 730 hours, in USD?
hint: Difference per hour, times 730, times ten.

prompt: Match each workload to the category of instance it belongs on.
hint: Which resource runs out first?

pairs.left: Video transcoding with every vCPU at 100%
A database reading its own local NVMe at very high rates
A bastion host idle most of the day
